desc:
The string words holds several lowercase words separated by single commas, for example "flower,flow,flight". Choose two different positions in this list and look at the longest prefix the two words have in common. Return the largest such length over all pairs of positions.

The same word may occur more than once in the list; two equal words (at different positions) share their whole length. If no two words share even their first letter, the answer is 0.

words = "flower,flow,flight"  ->  4   ("flower" and "flow" share "flow")
words = "dog,racecar,car"     ->  0
words = "ab,b,ab"             ->  2   (the two equal words "ab")
constraints: The list holds between 2 and 3,000 words
Every word has 1 to 50 lowercase English letters
The total length of words, commas included, is at most 30,000
hints: Checking every pair of words and computing their common prefix is correct. How many pairs are there when there are 3,000 words?
Think about where in alphabetical order two words with a long common prefix end up. Words that start with the same long prefix form a contiguous block.
Sort the words. The best pair is always two neighbours in the sorted order, so compare only adjacent words and keep the maximum common prefix length.
editorial: Comparing all pairs costs O(w2 · L) for w words of length up to L, which is too slow for thousands of words in a larger setting. The key observation is about sorted order: if words a ≤ b ≤ c are in sorted order, then lcp(a, c) = min(lcp(a, b), lcp(b, c)). So a pair that is not adjacent can never beat the adjacent pairs lying between them.

Therefore split the string on commas, sort the words, and take the maximum of lcp(words[i], words[i+1]) over neighbours. Equal words become neighbours and give their full length automatically. Sorting costs O(total length · log w) in the worst case, and the scan costs O(total length). This 'sort, then look at neighbours' trick is the basic idea behind suffix arrays as well.
time: O(T log w), T = total length
